focus: Choose present forms by meaning: states, activities and what a speaker is doing with their words.
objectives: Distinguish a present state from an activity in progress.
Notice when a verb changes meaning between simple and continuous forms.
Recognise sentences where both forms are possible.
Describe your own situation using the forms that express your intended meaning.

theory.title: Start with the meaning
paragraphs: The present simple can describe habits, facts and states. The present continuous can describe an activity in progress or a situation that is developing around now. The useful question is what the verb means here, rather than whether the sentence contains the word now.

A state can be true at this moment without becoming an activity. A preference, belief or possession will usually take a simple form. These are patterns of meaning, not a rule that every verb has only one possible tense.

examples.note: A present preference, expressed as a state.

examples.text: We are painting the quieter room this week.
examples.note: An activity happening during a limited period.

theory.title: Think, have and see
paragraphs: Think can express an opinion or the activity of considering something. Have can describe possession or an experience. See can mean understand or refer to meeting someone. Choose the form that fits that meaning.

examples.text: I think the smaller table is better. / I am thinking about where to put it.
Mina has a balcony. / Mina is having lunch on the balcony.
examples.note: Possession versus an activity or experience.

examples.text: I see your point. / I am seeing my tutor this afternoon.

theory.title: Measure, fit and appear
paragraphs: Measure can state a dimension or describe taking a measurement. Fit can describe having the right size or the activity of installing something. Appear can mean seem or describe taking part in a performance. The meaning changes before the grammar changes.

examples.text: The desk measures one metre across. / I am measuring the space beside it.
This lid fits the jar. / They are fitting new lights in the kitchen.
You appear to be ready. / Our neighbour is appearing in a local musical.

theory.title: Expect: a requirement or an awaited event
paragraphs: A simple form often expresses a general expectation or requirement. A continuous form often presents a particular event as something you are currently waiting for. Context matters: do not treat either pattern as the only possible use of expect.

examples.text: We expect everyone to label their equipment.
I am expecting a delivery this morning.
examples.note: A particular event that is currently anticipated.

theory.title: Words that perform an action
paragraphs: Sometimes saying a sentence is the action itself: you thank, admit, promise or refuse by speaking. The present simple is the usual form in direct statements of this kind.

This does not make the continuous form impossible in every context. It can describe an action or attitude in progress. Negative expressions such as I am not suggesting can also clarify what the speaker means at this moment.

examples.note: The speaker makes the apology by saying this.

examples.text: I am not promising that the repair will be quick.
examples.note: The speaker limits the commitment they are making.

theory.title: When both forms work
paragraphs: Some situations allow both forms. The simple presents an assessment or fact; the continuous draws attention to a current experience, change or temporary pattern. Both can be correct without being identical in emphasis.
In a question that asks for all correct answers, select every suitable option. In your own writing, choose the emphasis you actually want.

examples.text: The new arrangement works well. / The new arrangement is working well.
examples.note: A general assessment versus how it is working during the current period.

examples.text: I find these meetings useful. / I am finding these meetings useful.
examples.note: A judgement versus a current or developing experience.

explanations.u1-e1-q1: Here fit means be the right size. It describes a relationship between the jumper and its wearer, so use the present simple.
explanations.u1-e1-q2: Measure gives the dimensions of the room. It describes a fact about its size, rather than someone taking a measurement.
explanations.u1-e1-q3: Here measure is an activity: someone is finding the size of the window. The continuous form presents that activity as in progress.
explanations.u1-e1-q4: This is a general library requirement, rather than waiting for one particular delivery. The present simple expresses that expectation.
explanations.u1-e1-q5: Have describes physical features here. This is a state, so the third-person simple form is appropriate.
explanations.u1-e1-q6: Have a holiday describes an experience during the current period. The continuous form presents the holiday as in progress.
explanations.u1-e1-q7: Fit means install here. The builders are carrying out that activity today, which explains why the room is unavailable.
explanations.u1-e1-q8: Appear means seem in this sentence. It expresses an impression or judgement, rather than an activity such as performing on stage.
explanations.u1-e1-q9: Think of doing something means consider a possible plan here. The continuous form shows that the decision is still being considered.
explanations.u1-e1-q10: The speaker is currently waiting for a particular item to arrive. The continuous form presents this as an active expectation in the present situation.
explanations.u1-e2-q1: The speaker makes the admission by saying the sentence. The simple form is the expected direct use of confess here; a continuous form would put the act of confessing itself in focus.
explanations.u1-e2-q2: Both are possible. The simple gives an assessment of the sound. The continuous highlights how the performance is sounding now, especially compared with before.
explanations.u1-e2-q3: Prefer expresses a general preference motivated by a fear of flying. It is normally used in the simple form for this meaning.
explanations.u1-e2-q4: The reply refers to what the listener is imagining at this moment. The continuous form fits this current mental activity; the simple would suggest a general tendency.
explanations.u1-e2-q5: Both are possible. The simple states the expense as a fact. The continuous emphasises the expense accumulating during the present period. Every day does not automatically rule out the continuous.
explanations.u1-e2-q6: Believe reports the police's current view. This is a mental state, normally expressed with a simple form, rather than an activity in progress.
explanations.u1-e2-q7: Both negative forms are possible. The simple denies making that recommendation; the continuous clarifies what the speaker is not proposing in the current conversation.
explanations.u1-e2-q8: Consider means actively think about a possible decision. The continuous presents that decision-making as in progress; this is not the meaning regard as in a sentence such as I consider it useful.
explanations.u1-e2-q9: Both are possible. The simple expresses a judgement about the work. The continuous emphasises the speaker's current experience while doing it.
explanations.u1-e2-q10: In the intended reading, the speaker states a refusal directly, so the exercise uses the simple form. A continuous form can describe an ongoing refusal in a different context; it is not a universally forbidden combination.

listening.instruction: Listen and complete the missing verb form. Then listen again and notice whether it describes a state or an activity.

writing.prompt: Write a short update to a friend about your life this week. Include a fact about your usual life, an activity happening around now, an opinion, and a plan you are considering. Try using one verb in two different meanings. Aim for 60–120 words; this is a guide, not a pass-or-fail limit.
checklist: Does each simple or continuous form express the meaning I intend?
Have I included both a state and an activity in progress?
If I use think, have, see or another flexible verb, is its meaning clear?
Can I explain one choice where a different form would change the emphasis?

review.prompt: Lena ____ two bicycles: one for work and one for weekends. (have)
review.modelAnswer: Lena has two bicycles: one for work and one for weekends.
review.explanation: Have describes possession here. Use the present simple, with the third-person form.

review.prompt: Please wait a moment. I ____ the width of the doorway. (measure)
review.modelAnswer: Please wait a moment. I am measuring the width of the doorway.
review.explanation: Someone is taking a measurement now. This is an activity in progress, rather than a statement of size.

review.prompt: I ____ your point; your explanation makes sense to me.
review.modelAnswer: I see your point; your explanation makes sense to me.
review.explanation: See means understand here. It describes a mental state, not a meeting or another activity.

review.prompt: We have not decided yet. Right now, we ____ about a new name for our café. (think)
review.modelAnswer: We have not decided yet. Right now, we are thinking about a new name for our café.
review.explanation: Think describes an active process of considering possibilities. The decision is still being made.

review.prompt: At the moment, the new arrangement ____ well for everyone. Choose all suitable forms.
review.modelAnswer: At the moment, the new arrangement works / is working well for everyone.
review.explanation: Both forms are possible. The simple gives an assessment of the arrangement; the continuous highlights how it is functioning during the present period.
